 She’s Watching Inflation Hit 3.7% as Her Bills Keep Rising. Her 2027 Social Security Raise Is Already Locked at 3.6%
 Gerelyn Terzo Wed, November 4, 2026 at 2:02 PM EST 6 min read Quick Read 
 The 2027 Social Security COLA of 3.6% is already locked, and the gap versus 3.7% headline inflation amounts to roughly $2 a month for average retirees. 
 Medicare Part B premiums are deducted directly from Social Security checks, and rising premiums can significantly shrink the net benefit of any COLA raise. 
 Retirees should wait for their December Social Security notice before committing to new fixed costs, since it shows the real net deposit after deductions. 
 Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor) 
 Her electric bill went up. Her grocery total went up. Then she read that consumer prices climbed 3.7% in September, and she did the comparison almost every retiree does. Her 2027 Social Security raise is 3.6%, so it feels like she's behind before the first bigger check even shows up. 
 24/7 Wall St. Plenty of people feel the same way. The gap between a Social Security raise and actual household expenses can leave retirees feeling like they're falling behind even when their checks get bigger. When Social Security pays most of the monthly bills, every tenth of a point feels personal. 
 In dollars, though, that tenth of a point is small. For the average retiree's estimated $2,095 benefit, the difference between a 3.7% raise and a 3.6% raise is about $2 a month. The bigger pressures on her budget are coming from somewhere else. 
 Her Raise Came From a Different Inflation Gauge and a Fixed Three-Month Window 
 Social Security uses a different gauge from the headline inflation number: the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). It measures changes in prices but weights spending differently from the headline index. The raise compares the average of the July, August and September figures with the same three months a year earlier. 
 In 2026, those three monthly figures were 327.104, 328.481 and 330.654. Once that third-quarter average is published, the math is finished.

 Neither index is designed specifically around retirees' spending. A separate research measure, the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E), tracks inflation for households with people 62 and older, giving more weight to expenses such as housing and medical care. Even that measure can't capture what any individual retiree actually spends. 
 What 3.6% Actually Adds to Her Monthly Deposit 
 Social Security estimates the average retired worker's benefit will rise from $2,095 to $2,170, about $75 more a month. 
 A widow or widower living alone goes from $1,867 to $1,919 on average. 
 Her own raise is her own benefit times 3.6%. If her check is $1,500, that works out to about $54 more each month before anything comes out of it. 
 A major deduction is Medicare Part B, which usually comes straight out of her Social Security check. For 2026, the standard premium rose from $185 to $202.90, a $17.90 increase that ate part of that year's 2.8% raise. 
 The 2027 premium is still pending. If it rises again, the deposit in her bank account will grow by less than 3.6%. Retirees with higher incomes pay extra Medicare fees on top of that, starting above $109,000 for single taxpayers under the 2026 brackets. 
 Fall Price Spikes Can't Reopen the January 2027 Raise 
 Price jumps in October, November and December won't change the raise that starts with January 2027 checks. That raise is final. Higher prices from this fall carry into the price level behind next year's July through September figures, so they show up in the 2028 calculation if they stick around. 
 That built-in delay works in both directions. The 8.7% raise for 2023 came after prices had been climbing for more than a year. The 3.2% raise for 2024 followed as inflation cooled. The formula eventually reflects earlier price increases, but that doesn't mean every retiree's purchasing power fully recovers. 
 Build Next Year's Budget From Her Own Notice 
 Her most useful number for 2027 is the net deposit printed on her own Social Security notice, which arrives in December and also appears in her online account. It shows the new gross benefit, the Medicare deduction and what actually lands in the bank. Using that figure instead of a headline inflation rate gives her a plan built on real dollars. 
 The hardest mistake to undo is signing up for a new fixed cost, like a pricier insurance plan or a higher rent renewal, based on a raise she hasn't seen yet. Waiting a few weeks for the notice costs nothing. If the numbers come in lower than she hoped, looking at her own biggest expenses (housing, medical, insurance) will usually tell her more than any national index can. Medicare in particular hides more costs than its sticker price suggests, from Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) fees to coverage gaps, and we mapped the full list in a free guide here. 
 Every household's benefit, Medicare costs and spending are a little different, so her neighbor's raise may not look like hers.
